title: Why Zebulun and Naphtali Were Called More Honorable Than Others
paragraphs: Why Zebulun and Naphtali Were Called More Honorable Than Others
There are names in Scripture that most people read too quickly.
Names buried in genealogies. Names hidden between wars. Names mentioned once in prophecy and forgotten by the next chapter.
But heaven never wastes names.
And sometimes the tribes nobody expected became the tribes God chose to honor publicly.
Zebulun. Naphtali.
Two tribes from the northern region of Israel. Two tribes constantly threatened. Two tribes exposed to invasion. Two tribes overlooked politically. Two tribes surrounded by darkness.
Yet somehow... when God spoke through Isaiah about the coming glory of the Messiah... He mentioned them first.
Not Judah. Not Benjamin. Not Levi.
Zebulun and Naphtali.
That alone should make every serious Bible reader stop and ask: Why?
Why would God intentionally spotlight these two tribes? Why did Scripture connect them to honor, light, glory, courage, and Messiah Himself? Why did Jesus begin His ministry there?
Because buried inside their story is one of the greatest revelations about how God chooses people.
And maybe one of the deepest comforts for wounded believers.
Because God has always loved bringing light into places everybody else gave up on.
Isaiah 9:1–2 says:

“Nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations. The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.”
Most people quote this at Christmas and never slow down enough to realize what God was actually saying.
This was not random geography.
This was redemption.
The Hebrew phrase for “great light” is:
אוֹר גָּדוֹל
'Or gadol.
Not a weak light. Not temporary inspiration. Not emotional positivity.
A massive divine light. A heaven-breaking light. A covenant light.
And where did God send it first?
Into wounded territory.
Zebulun and Naphtali were the first regions devastated by Assyrian invasion.
2 Kings 15:29 records that Tiglath-Pileser attacked these northern territories first.
They suffered humiliation before others. They experienced darkness before others. They were exposed before others.
And that matters.
Because many people assume honor means protection from suffering.
But biblically... God often honors people by trusting them with battle first.
That changes everything.
The Hebrew word often connected to honor is:
כָּבֵד
Kaved.
It literally means “weighty,” “heavy,” “significant,” or “glorious.”
Honor in Scripture is not celebrity. Honor is spiritual weight.
God gave Zebulun and Naphtali spiritual weight because they endured darkness without losing prophetic destiny.
Most people cannot handle prolonged darkness without becoming bitter.
These tribes did.
And God remembered.
This is one of the most misunderstood patterns in all Scripture:
The places attacked hardest are often the places God plans to reveal Himself through most powerfully.
The enemy strikes territories prophetically.
That means some people reading this have hated themselves for wounds that may actually reveal where heaven intends to shine brightest.
Your deepest warfare may be connected to your deepest assignment.
The enemy does not waste attacks.
Neither does God.
When Matthew quoted Isaiah concerning Jesus beginning His ministry in Galilee, he intentionally connected Christ directly to Zebulun and Naphtali.
Matthew 4:13–16 says:
“And leaving Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet...”
Jesus could have launched His ministry anywhere.
Jerusalem would have made political sense. The temple would have made religious sense. The capital would have made strategic sense.
But heaven chose wounded territory.
Again.
Do you see the pattern?
God intentionally starts glory where shame once lived.
This is why the Gospel is so offensive to pride.
Because God repeatedly bypasses human systems of importance.
He chooses:
David over Saul. Joseph in prison. Gideon hiding. Ruth the outsider. Mary from Nazareth. Fishermen over scholars. The cross over the throne.
And Zebulun and Naphtali over religious prestige.
The religious mind struggles with this because religion believes honor is earned through visibility.
But Scripture shows honor is often hidden inside endurance.
Some of the most honored people in heaven were barely noticed on earth.
And some believers reading this have secretly believed:
“If God loved me, my life would not have been this painful.”
But Zebulun and Naphtali tell another story.
Sometimes the first territory attacked becomes the first territory illuminated.
That is not rejection.
That is prophetic positioning.
In Genesis 49, Jacob prophetically blesses his sons before death.
When he speaks over Zebulun, he says:
“Zebulun shall dwell at the haven of the sea; and he shall be for an haven of ships.”
The Hebrew phrase carries imagery of openness, access, commerce, movement, and connection.
Zebulun became associated with reaching outward.
Naphtali, meanwhile, receives this blessing:
“Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words.”
The Hebrew phrase for “goodly words” can imply beautiful speech, fruitful declarations, elegant expression.
Freedom. Expression. Movement.
One tribe connected to expansion. One tribe connected to release.
Then centuries later... Jesus walks directly into their region carrying the Kingdom of God.
Nothing in Scripture is accidental.
Not geography. Not timing. Not tribal placement. Not prophecy.
Even the location of Christ’s ministry reveals God’s heart toward broken regions.
Galilee itself carried stigma.
In John 1:46, Nathanael asked:
“Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?”
That was not a compliment.
Galilee was often viewed as spiritually compromised, culturally mixed, and less prestigious.
Yet Jesus intentionally rooted Himself there.
Why?
Because God loves invading despised places with undeniable glory.
And honestly... this destroys human pride.
Because many believers still think God moves most powerfully through polished people.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals God moving through surrendered people.
There is a difference.
One performs. One depends.
One seeks applause. One seeks Christ.
And Zebulun and Naphtali remind us that God can transform devastated territory into holy ground.
This is why Isaiah’s prophecy matters so deeply.
The people walking in darkness saw great light.
Notice:
They were still walking.
They were wounded... but still moving.
Confused... but still moving.
Surrounded by darkness... but still moving.
And then the light came.
Somebody reading this is exhausted because you expected God to remove the darkness immediately.
But many times God develops endurance before revelation.
The Greek word used for endurance in the New Testament is:
ὑπομονή
Hypomonē.
It means steadfastness. Remaining under pressure. Refusing to quit. Faithfulness under burden.
Zebulun and Naphtali carried hypomonē before the Messiah arrived.
And some believers are one season away from seeing why the warfare was so intense.
The enemy wanted them to quit before the light appeared.
That is still happening today.
Some people abandoned prayer too early. Some surrendered purity too early. Some walked away from God too early. Some lost hope too early.
And hell celebrated prematurely.
Because what looked like devastation was actually preparation.
The Gospel changes how suffering is interpreted.
Without Christ, suffering looks meaningless.
With Christ, suffering can become transformation.
Romans 8:18 says:
“For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.”
Notice Paul did not deny suffering.
He compared it.
That changes everything.
The glory outweighs the pain.
The resurrection outweighs the cross. The restoration outweighs the betrayal. The healing outweighs the wound. The Kingdom outweighs the darkness.
And Zebulun and Naphtali became prophetic proof.
God did not forget wounded territory.
He visited it personally.
There is another detail many people miss.
When Deborah and Barak fought Sisera in Judges 4 and 5, Zebulun and Naphtali were among the tribes that courageously entered battle.
Judges 5:18 says:
“Zebulun and Naphtali were a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field.”
That verse is explosive.
Because many tribes hesitated. Some stayed comfortable. Some remained distant.
But Zebulun and Naphtali risked themselves.
The Hebrew imagery carries sacrificial courage.
Not convenience. Not safety.
Courage.
That matters spiritually.
Because heaven notices who remains faithful when obedience becomes costly.
Modern Christianity often celebrates platforms.
But Scripture celebrates surrender.
The Kingdom of God was never built by comfortable spectators.
It was built by surrendered people willing to carry crosses.
And these tribes did.
No wonder God later associated them with light.
People who survive darkness with faith intact become dangerous to hell.
There are believers reading this who feel disqualified because of previous pain.
But the Bible repeatedly shows God using scarred territory.
Thomas doubted. Peter failed. Moses stuttered. David fell. Paul persecuted Christians. Mary Magdalene carried deep torment before freedom.
Yet Jesus redeemed all of it.
The enemy loves convincing wounded believers that they are permanently unusable.
But Christ specializes in resurrection.
Not improvement.
Resurrection.
There is a difference.
Improvement modifies. Resurrection restores life where death existed.
And that is exactly what happened prophetically in Zebulun and Naphtali.
Light invaded devastated territory.
The Messiah walked into forgotten regions.
Heaven honored places others dismissed.
And maybe that is why this story hits so personally for so many people.
Because deep down... most people know what it feels like to carry hidden darkness.
Some hide depression behind smiles. Some hide addiction behind church attendance. Some hide lust behind theology. Some hide exhaustion behind productivity. Some hide grief behind humor.
But Jesus still walks toward dark places.
Not away from them.
That is the Gospel.
John 1:5 says:
“And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.”
The Greek word for “comprehended” is:
κατέλαβεν
Katelaben.
It can mean overcome, overpower, seize, suppress.
Darkness could not overpower the Light.
That means your darkness is not stronger than Christ.
Your shame is not stronger than Christ. Your addiction is not stronger than Christ. Your past is not stronger than Christ. Your fear is not stronger than Christ.
The Light still wins.
Always.
And maybe somebody needed to hear that today more than they needed another motivational speech.
Because motivational speeches cannot resurrect dead souls.
Only Jesus can.
This is why the Gospel is not self-help.
It is supernatural rebirth.
The Greek phrase Jesus used in John 3 for “born again” is:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν
Gennēthē anōthen.
Born from above.
Not behavior modification. Not image management. Not religious cosmetics.
A new heart. A new spirit. A new creation.
And the same God who brought light into Zebulun and Naphtali still brings light into shattered lives today.
That is why no testimony is too broken. No past too filthy. No addiction too strong. No family too damaged. No mind too tormented.
Jesus still walks into Galilee.
He still enters wounded regions.
He still calls ordinary people.
And He still changes everything.
Maybe that is why this story refuses to die.
Because people recognize themselves in it.
The forgotten. The ashamed. The exhausted. The attacked. The spiritually numb. The ones wondering if God still sees them.
Zebulun and Naphtali answer:
Yes.
God sees wounded territory.
And sometimes... He chooses it first.
The places you thought disqualified you may become the exact places where Christ reveals His glory most powerfully.
